etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English implien, emplien, borrowed from Old French emplier, from Latin implicare (“to infold, involve”), from in (“in”) + plicare (“to fold”). Doublet of employ and implicate.

definitions.definition: (transitive, of a proposition) to have as a necessary consequence; to lead to (something) as a consequence

quote.citation: 2016, Grigoriy Blekherman, Daniel Plaumann, Rainer Sinn, Cynthia Vinzant, “Low-Rank Sum-of-Squares Representations on Varieties of Minimal Degree”, in arXiv‎[1]:
quote.text: Our upper bound is the best possible, and it implies the existence of low-rank factorizations of positive semidefinite bivariate matrix polynomials and representations of biforms as sums of few squares.

definitions.definition: (transitive, of a person) to suggest by logical inference
(transitive, of a person or proposition) to hint; to insinuate; to suggest tacitly and avoid a direct statement

quote.text: The wrongminded notion of the feminist movement which implied it was anti-male carried with it the wrongminded assumption that all female space would necessarily be an environment where patriarchy and sexist thinking would be absent.
Naturally, the river wasn't wrinkled or creased at all— wrong words, implying something unfluid like skin, something unenduring, prey to age.

quote.citation: 2022, R. F. Kuang, Babel, HarperVoyager, page 470:
quote.text: Both French and English had once used parcel to refer to pieces of land that made up an estate, but when it evolved to imply an item of business in both, it retained its connotations of small fragmentariness in French, whereas in English it simply meant a package.
